strengths: Novel application of VAR models to generative classification with clear motivation and practical value
Significant computational efficiency gains (160× speedup) while maintaining reasonable accuracy on ImageNet-100
Well-designed technical contributions: likelihood smoothing elegantly addresses quantization artifacts; partial-scale pruning effectively exploits VAR's multi-scale architecture
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple distribution-shift datasets with thorough ablation studies
Interesting secondary contributions including visual explainability via token-wise PMI and inherent resistance to catastrophic forgetting
Honest reporting of limitations (robustness properties don't transfer from diffusion to VAR)
Strong presentation quality and commitment to reproducibility with detailed implementation information
weaknesses: Significant accuracy gap with discriminative baselines (2-5% lower than ResNets/ViTs) undermines practical applicability for classification tasks
Limited technical novelty: likelihood smoothing is straightforward sampling; partial-scale pruning follows naturally from architecture; CCA is from concurrent work
Expected robustness improvements from prior generative classifier work do not transfer to VAR, eliminating a key theoretical motivation
Fundamental unresolved generation-discrimination trade-off: larger models improve generation but degrade classification (d30: 64.96% accuracy), limiting scalability
Severely limited experimental scope: evaluation only on ImageNet-100 (100 classes) rather than full ImageNet-1000; class-incremental learning uses only 10 classes
Incomplete explainability analysis: no quantitative evaluation or comparison to other interpretability methods; unclear if PMI is superior to simpler alternatives
Experimental fairness concerns: diffusion baselines estimated rather than directly measured on same hardware; three-stage procedure appears specifically engineered while baselines use fixed settings
Missing comparisons to other autoregressive models and limited analysis of when VAR classifiers should be preferred over alternatives
Root cause of likelihood smoothing requirement not analyzed; suggests base model's likelihood may be miscalibrated, creating conceptual tension with generative classifier theory

strengths: Addresses practical efficiency challenge of generative classifiers with 160× speedup over diffusion methods
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple distribution-shift datasets provides broader perspective than prior work
Clever exploitation of VAR's multi-scale architecture for partial-scale candidate pruning
Identifies and empirically demonstrates a fundamental trade-off between model size and classification accuracy (Appendix C)
Good reproducibility with provided pseudocode, implementation details, and public code references
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: straightforward application of Bayes' rule to VAR models with incremental engineering contributions
Critical: robustness property does not transfer to VAR from diffusion models, contradicting key motivation for generative classifiers; improvements only on ImageNet-A
Significant accuracy gap vs discriminative baselines (4.88% vs ViT-B/16) substantially limits practical applicability
Scalability problem not fundamentally solved; linear complexity in number of classes remains; evaluation limited to 100 classes not full 1000-class ImageNet
Fundamental unresolved trade-off: larger VAR models dramatically hurt classification (88.68% → 71.64% with CCA from d16 to d30); identified problem (class-information dilution) lacks solution
Class-incremental learning evaluation is weak (only 10 classes, 2 tasks) with unfair comparison setup; insufficient evidence of practical advantage
Likelihood smoothing adds substantial computational cost back (doubles inference time), partially offsetting efficiency gains
Misleading framing: VAR models are not actually more efficient at classification than discriminative methods
Limited justification for when to use this approach over simply using ViT-B/16, which achieves 94.20% vs 89.32%
Hand-tuned three-stage pruning with different parameters (K', σ, sample counts) appears ad-hoc; limited ablation on sensitivity

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: VAR models offer tractable likelihoods avoiding the computational overhead of diffusion-based classifiers (dozens to hundreds of function evaluations)
Novel perspective opening a new research direction: First serious study of VAR-based generative classifiers, providing insights distinct from diffusion-dominated literature
Practical engineering contributions: Likelihood smoothing and partial-scale pruning are well-motivated, simple, and effective; 160× speedup over diffusion classifiers is significant
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple distribution-shift datasets, fair baselines (ResNets, ViTs, IBINN, diffusion), thorough ablation studies, and good reproducibility effort
Honest scientific reporting: Transparently reporting that VAR classifiers don't exhibit robustness properties of diffusion models clarifies which properties are method-specific
Interesting additional properties: Visual explainability via token-wise PMI is novel and well-visualized; inherent resistance to catastrophic forgetting is valuable for continual learning
Well-controlled experimental setup: Consistent 256-resolution models, controlled class subsets, good implementation details in appendix
weaknesses: Significant accuracy gap: A-VARC+ achieves 89.32% vs 94.20% for ViT-B/16 on ImageNet-100 (5% drop); this substantially limits practical adoption and undermines motivation for generative classifiers

Concerning generative-discriminative trade-off (Appendix C): Accuracy degrades significantly with larger models (VAR-d30: 64.96%), suggesting poor scalability; this critical limitation is buried in appendix rather than prominently discussed
Heavy dependence on CCA finetuning: Without CCA only 83.30% accuracy, with CCA 89.72%; contribution conflates VAR-specific improvements with general benefits from concurrent work Chen et al. (2024b)

Limited validation of key claims: Robustness doesn't transfer from diffusion (undermining motivation); visual explainability lacks comparison with established methods and quantitative evaluation; catastrophic forgetting validated only on 10 classes/2 tasks
Limited evaluation scope: Only ImageNet-100 subsets evaluated, not full ImageNet-1000; no evaluation on other domains; full-scale validation would be more convincing
Hyperparameter choices not well justified: Noise variance σ=0.1, smoothing samples S=10, three-stage configuration lack ablation studies; unclear if choices generalize to other datasets
Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; '<1% accuracy drop' claim not formally validated; some experiments run once only
Unfair comparison elements: Different model architectures (VAR-d16 vs DiT-XL/2), different procedural stages, heterogeneous hardware platforms for runtime measurements complicate direct comparison

Unresolved fundamental questions: Paper doesn't adequately explain when practitioners should choose generative over discriminative classifiers; the robustness properties that motivated generative classifiers don't appear in VAR approach

strengths: Addresses real practical problem: 89× efficiency improvement over diffusion-based generative classifiers with comparable accuracy on ImageNet-100

Technical approach is sound and well-motivated: likelihood smoothing handles instability, partial-scale pruning cleverly exploits VAR's multi-scale structure, Figure 2 convincingly demonstrates effectiveness

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple distribution-shift datasets (ImageNetV2, ImageNetR, ImageNet-Sketch, ObjectNet, ImageNet-A) with appropriate baselines (ResNet, ViT, IBINN, diffusion classifiers)
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2, 5, 6) clearly show contribution of each component with detailed analysis
Reproducibility is strong with detailed implementation details, class lists, pseudo-code, and promise to release code

Additional contributions beyond efficiency: token-wise mutual information provides quantitatively-evaluated visual explanations, demonstrates class-incremental learning without catastrophic forgetting
Well-written paper with clear motivation, logical flow, and effective presentation
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: likelihood smoothing is straightforward perturbation-averaging, partial-scale pruning is natural application of architecture, CCA finetuning from concurrent work (Chen et al. 2024b); primarily engineering contribution

Significant scale limitations: restricted to ImageNet-100 (100 classes with 50 samples) rather than standard ImageNet-1000; distribution-shift experiments use only 10 samples per class; no assessment of real-world large-scale applicability
Substantial performance gap vs. discriminative models remains unaddressed: A-VARC+ achieves 89.32% on ImageNet-100 vs. 94.20% for ViT-B/16 (5% gap); discriminative models dominate on all variants

Negative result undermines core claims: VAR classifiers do NOT inherit distribution-shift robustness reported for diffusion models, suggesting robustness comes from denoising paradigm not generative objective, limiting advantages over discriminative approaches

Fundamental generative-discriminative trade-off: accuracy drops sharply with model size (83.30% for d16 → 64.96% for d30), with CCA only partially mitigating (71.64%); prevents scaling to larger backbones

Likelihood smoothing design choices lack principled justification: re-quantization in discrete space may not preserve perceptual similarity; no comparison with alternative smoothing approaches; adds 2× computational overhead (Table 2)

Visual explainability results are mixed: LIME still outperforms TMI on A-VARC insertion metric (0.979 vs 0.845); improvement in A-VARC+ appears attributable to CCA finetuning generally rather than TMI specifically
Class-incremental learning evaluation insufficient: only proof-of-concept on 10 classes with 2 tasks; no comparison with established class-incremental methods; doesn't use standard benchmarks
Evaluation inconsistencies: different subsampling strategies across datasets (50 vs 10 samples) complicate comparisons; anomalously high GFLOP values for DC-MF (286287.6) raise measurement concerns
Strong dependency on concurrent work: improvement heavily driven by CCA finetuning (A-VARC 83.30% → +smoothing 88.26% → +CCA 88.68%); reduces independent contribution claim

Missing critical experiments: no evaluation on full ImageNet-1000; no comparison with other efficiency approaches (distillation, pruning, quantization); limited robustness evaluation despite mention in related work

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing computational inefficiency of diffusion-based generative classifiers
Impressive computational efficiency gains (89× reduction in GFLOPs compared to diffusion classifiers)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets with appropriate baselines and ablations
Clear presentation with detailed implementation details, pseudo-code, and reproducibility information
Technically sound approach with reasonable engineering solutions (likelihood smoothing, partial-scale pruning)
Exploration of multiple model properties including visual explainability and class-incremental learning
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core techniques (smoothing, two-stage pruning, CCA) are adaptations of existing methods rather than fundamental contributions
Critical evaluation limitation: all results use ImageNet-100 (100 classes), not full ImageNet-1000; undermines scalability claims and practical significance

Fundamental trade-off between generative and discriminative performance (Appendix D) suggests poor scaling: accuracy drops from 83.30% (d16) to 64.96% (d30), indicating the approach doesn't scale with model size

Promised distribution-shift robustness does not transfer to VAR-based classifiers across most datasets (ImageNetV2, ImageNetR, ObjectNet, ImageNet-Sketch), contradicting motivation for generative approaches

Modest accuracy improvements with high dependency on CCA finetuning (0.98% below DiT despite added complexity); unclear why practitioners would use this over superior discriminative models (ViT-B/16: 94.20%)
Visual explainability claims overstate results: LIME outperforms TMI on insertion metric for A-VARC; quantitative evaluation limited to insertion/deletion metrics without user studies

Class-incremental learning evaluation is underdeveloped: only proof-of-concept on 10 classes with marginal improvements over diffusion (77.4% vs 76.0%), no comparison with standard incremental learning methods
Hyperparameter sensitivity: sharp performance cliff with likelihood smoothing variance (σ=1.0 drops to 39.54%), limited guidance on hyperparameter selection
Unclear practical utility: no articulated use cases where VAR classifiers are preferable to faster, more accurate discriminative alternatives
Incomplete investigation of robustness failure: paper acknowledges VAR lacks distribution-shift robustness but doesn't investigate why or propose solutions
Experimental rigor concerns: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; subsampling to 10 samples per class limits reproducibility

strengths: Significant practical efficiency improvement (89× reduction in computational cost) with near-comparable accuracy to diffusion classifiers on ImageNet-100
Well-motivated problem formulation addressing the computational bottleneck of diffusion-based generative classifiers
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple baselines, diverse distribution-shift datasets, thorough ablations, and fair comparison setup
Technically sound design choices with clear empirical motivation (likelihood smoothing addresses token quantization brittleness; partial-scale pruning exploits multi-scale architecture)
Novel secondary contributions in visual explainability (token-wise mutual information) and natural class-incremental learning without replay data
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation specifics, pseudo-code, dataset specifications, and promised code release
Clear presentation with effective motivation, good visualizations, and logical flow
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: likelihood smoothing is straightforward; partial-scale candidate pruning is adapted from Li et al. (2023); CCA finetuning is entirely from Chen et al. (2024b). Contribution is primarily engineering rather than novel methodology

Unfulfilled robustness claims: despite motivation emphasizing generative classifier robustness, VAR-based classifiers show no advantage on most distribution-shift datasets and significantly underperform discriminative models on ImageNet-Sketch (34% vs 52% for ViT)
Serious model-size scalability issues (Appendix D, not adequately addressed in main text): accuracy degrades catastrophically from 83.30% (d16) to 64.96% (d30); CCA only partially mitigates to 71.64%
Accuracy-efficiency tradeoff is not clear-cut: 1% drop on ImageNet-100 is non-trivial; ViT-B/16 achieves 94.20% at 16.9 GFLOPs (better accuracy with similar final efficiency)

Limited evaluation scope: ImageNet-100 is a small subset; class-incremental learning evaluation uses only 10 classes and 2 tasks (too limited); no evaluation on other domains (CIFAR-10/100, fine-grained classification)

Explainability benefits not inherent to VAR: token-wise mutual information underperforms LIME on A-VARC (Table 3) and only excels after CCA finetuning; failure cases show TMI can be misleading for visually similar classes

Incomplete technical analysis: limited insight into why VAR's next-scale prediction benefits classification; three-stage procedure (K=10,3,1) appears ad-hoc; hyperparameter σ shows extreme sensitivity (88.26% → 39.54% for σ=1.0)

Missing critical analysis: no wall-clock inference time (only GFLOPs); no scalability analysis to full ImageNet (1000 classes); efficiency comparison doesn't account for variable sampling in diffusion classifiers
